\chapter{Numbers Eleven to Twenty and Weather}
\label{ch:ta-numbers-and-weather}
\hlchaptermodality{20}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count eleven to twenty as the transparent compounds they are, and say what the weather is doing.}

Take vāṉilai apart into vāṉam plus nilai, then report the weather with mazhai peykiRathu.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ta{பதினொன்று} — \ta{இருபது}]{\ta{பதினொன்று}–\ta{இருபது} — shared Dravidian patterns}

\label{lesson:TA-C20-pathinondru-irupathu}



\begin{quote}
Here's how this arc closes: four completely different approaches to \textquotedblleft{}twenty\textquotedblright{} across Sanskrit, Latin, Arabic — and then all four Dravidian languages quietly agreeing on the exact same compositional idea.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{பதினொன்று}–\ta{பத்தொன்பது} — \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} + digit}
Tamil's teens echo \textbf{\ta{பத்து}} (\emph{pathu}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ten}\textquotedblright{}) plus each digit — \textbf{\ta{பதினொன்று}} (\emph{patiṉoṉḏṟu}, 11), \textbf{\ta{பன்னிரண்டு}} (\emph{paṉṉiraṇḍu}, 12), and onward through \textbf{\ta{பத்தொன்பது}} (\emph{pattoṉbatu}, 19) — the same digit-plus- ten-echo compounding you've now seen across Kannada, Telugu, and Malayalam.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{இருபது} — transparently \textquotedblleft{}two-tens\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\ta{இருபது}} (\emph{irupathu}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{twenty}\textquotedblright{}) = \textbf{\ta{இரு}} (\emph{iru}, an older word for \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two},\textquotedblright{} alongside the everyday \textbf{\ta{இரண்டு}} \emph{iraṇḍu}) + \textbf{\ta{பத்து}} (\emph{pathu}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ten}\textquotedblright{}) — fully transparent as \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two-tens},\textquotedblright{} matching \textbf{Malayalam's} own \emph{irupathu} almost letter-for-letter.

\begin{culture}
This closes the numbers arc with a genuinely clean pattern. All four major Dravidian languages build \textquotedblleft{}twenty\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{same} compositional way — some (Tamil, Malayalam) keeping it fully transparent on the surface today, some (Kannada) with the same compositional origin but no longer visibly matching the modern standalone words for \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}ten,\textquotedblright{} some (Telugu) worn down further but most likely from the same root. Compare that to the other three families you've met: Sanskrit's \textbf{\dv{विंशति}} (\emph{vimshati}), Latin's \textbf{vīgintī}, and Arabic's \textbf{\ar{عشرون}} (\emph{ʿishrūn}) are each their \textbf{own} special, non-compositional word for twenty — none built transparently from \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} the way Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam all do.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}patiṉoṉḏṟu, paṉṉiraṇḍu\textquotedblright{} — 11, 12
  \item \textquotedblleft{}iru\textquotedblright{} — an older word for two, \textquotedblleft{}pathu\textquotedblright{} — ten
  \item \textquotedblleft{}irupathu\textquotedblright{} — twenty, \textquotedblleft{}two-tens,\textquotedblright{} transparent
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two pieces build \textbf{\ta{இருபது}} (twenty)? (\textbf{\ta{இரு}} \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{\ta{பத்து}} \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two-tens}.\textquotedblright{}) Do all four major Dravidian languages build \textquotedblleft{}twenty\textquotedblright{} the same compositional way? (\textbf{Yes} — Tamil and Malayalam keep it fully transparent today; Kannada shares the same compositional origin but its modern \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{}/\textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} words no longer visibly match; Telugu's is worn down further but most likely the same root.) Do Sanskrit, Latin, or Arabic build their word for twenty this way? (\textbf{No} — each has its own special, non-compositional standalone word instead.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vāṉilai]{\ta{வானிலை} — \textquotedblleft{}the standing of the sky,\textquotedblright{} most likely all native}

\label{lesson:TA-C20-vaanilai}



\begin{quote}
You've now seen a Persian+Sanskrit hybrid (Kannada), a pure Sanskrit compound (Telugu), and a Sanskrit compound echoing \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} (Malayalam). Tamil most likely breaks the pattern one more time — with a word built entirely from native pieces.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வானிலை} — vaanam + nilai}
\textbf{\ta{வானிலை}} (\emph{vāṉilai}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{weather}\textquotedblright{} — built from:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{வானம்}} (\emph{vāṉam}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{sky}\textquotedblright{}) — most likely a \textbf{native Dravidian} word, with confirmed cognates in \textbf{Kannada} \textbf{\ka{ಬಾನು}} (\emph{bānu}, \textquotedblleft{}sky\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{Telugu} \textbf{\te{వాన}} (\emph{vāna}, \textquotedblleft{}rain,\textquotedblright{} from the same sky/rain-cloud root) — distinct from the Sanskrit sky word \emph{ākāśa} that those same two languages use elsewhere.
  \item \textbf{\ta{நிலை}} (\emph{nilai}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{state, standing, condition}\textquotedblright{}) — from \textbf{\ta{நில்}} (\emph{nil}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to stand}\textquotedblright{}), one of Tamil's most basic native verb roots.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{vāṉilai} literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the standing of the sky}\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the sky's state}\textquotedblright{} — and unlike its three Dravidian cousins, neither piece here is a Sanskrit or Persian/Arabic loan. (Treat \textquotedblleft{}native\textquotedblright{} as the best current account rather than a fully settled fact, the same hedge every native-word claim here deserves — but both pieces are independently well-attested as old, native Dravidian vocabulary.)

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மழை} \ta{பெய்கிறது} — \textquotedblleft{}rain is falling\textquotedblright{}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{மழை} \ta{பெய்கிறது}.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's raining.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{rain is falling}.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{mazhai peykiRathu} — from \textbf{\ta{பெய்}} \emph{pey}, \textquotedblleft{}to fall/pour,\textquotedblright{} specifically used for rain.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vāṉilai\textquotedblright{} — weather, \textquotedblleft{}the standing of the sky\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vāṉam\textquotedblright{} — sky, \textquotedblleft{}nilai\textquotedblright{} — state, from \textquotedblleft{}nil,\textquotedblright{} to stand
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mazhai peykiRathu\textquotedblright{} — it's raining, \textquotedblleft{}rain is falling\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \textbf{\ta{வானிலை}}, and what does the whole word literally mean? (\textbf{\ta{வானம்}}, \textquotedblleft{}sky,\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{\ta{நிலை}}, \textquotedblleft{}state/standing\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the standing of the sky}.\textquotedblright{}) Is either piece a Sanskrit or Persian/Arabic loan, unlike Kannada, Telugu, or Malayalam's weather words? (\textbf{Most likely not} — both pieces are native Dravidian.) What Tamil word does Malayalam's \emph{mazha} match for \textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\ta{மழை}}, \emph{mazhai}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ya]{\ta{ய} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TA-S124-letter-ya}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ta{◌ே} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{ய}}
\textbf{\ta{ய}} — \emph{ya}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{y}, it is \textbf{ya}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ta{ய} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{பெயர்}} \emph{peyar} — name
  \item \textbf{\ta{என்} \ta{பெயர்} …} \emph{eṉ peyar …} — my name is… (with no \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\ta{பரவாயில்லை}} \emph{paravāyillai} — it's okay / no problem / you're welcome
  \item \textbf{\ta{போய்} \ta{வருகிறேன்}} \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ} — goodbye (lit. \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ta{ய} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ta{ய} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ta{ய} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ta{பெயர்}  ·  \ta{வணக்கம்}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ta{ய} three times, saying \emph{ya} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ta{ய} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ta{ய}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ya}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
